# Use case 2: protein co-abundance networks from single-cell proteomics

Here, we will use __GraphExperiment__ to store a protein co-abundance network
inferred from mass spectrometry-based single-cell proteomics (SCP) data.
Co-abundance networks are typically inferred with the WGCNA algorithm
[@langfelder2008wgcna], which has been widely used in large-scale
proteomics studies [@johnson2022large; @seyfried2017multi], because
soft-thresholding and topological overlap-based module detection are more
robust than simple correlation thresholds.

We will use the data set from @khan2024dynamics, available in the
__scpdata__ package [@vanderaa2023current], which contains SCP data for 421
MCF-10A cells undergoing epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) triggered by
TGF-$\beta$, with cells collected at days 0, 3, and 9.

SCP data (as scRNA-seq data) are very sparse, which deflates correlations
and makes co-abundance network inference unreliable. A common
approach to handle sparsity is to aggregate similar cells into
*metacells* before network inference [@morabito2023hdwgcna],
which is what we will do here.

```{r here}
#| message: false
#| eval: true

library(here)
library(GraphExperiment)
library(scpdata)
library(QFeatures)
library(BioNERO)
library(bluster)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggraph)

set.seed(123) # for reproducibility
```

## Data description

The data are stored in a `QFeatures` object [@gatto2025qfeatures] with
quantitative data at the PSM, peptide, and protein levels. Here, we will
only use the protein-level data, without imputation of missing values.

```{r}
# Load data
qf <- khan2023()
qf

# Get protein-level data with sample metadata
prot <- getWithColData(qf, "proteins_unimputed")
rm(qf) # free memory

prot
```

Let's have a look at the available *colData* variables, and the proportion
of missing values in our *assay*.

```{r}
# Quick check on colData variables
colData(prot)
table(prot$SampleType)

# Proportion of missing values
mean(is.na(assay(prot)))

# Proportion of missing values in proteins that are missing in all cells of a TMT set
na_in_blocks <- sapply(split(colnames(prot), prot$Set), function(cells) {
    na <- is.na(assay(prot)[, cells, drop = FALSE])
    sum(rowSums(na) == length(cells)) * length(cells)
})
sum(na_in_blocks) / sum(is.na(assay(prot)))
```

About 80% of the values are missing, and nearly all missing values occur
in proteins that are missing in all cells of a TMT set (i.e., an MS run).
Thus, missingness is mostly determined by which peptides were selected for
fragmentation and identified in each run, not by low abundances in
individual cells [@vanderaa2023revisiting]. This has
important implications for how we handle missing values. First,
imputation methods that assume left-censored data (e.g., MinProb) are not
suitable, as they would assign artificially low values to all cells of a
set, creating spurious co-abundance among proteins that are missing in the
same sets. This is aggravated by the fact that values are log-transformed
*relative* abundances centered on each protein's mean, so that low values do
not indicate low absolute abundances. Second, the data must be corrected for
batch effects (i.e., differences between TMT sets). Hence, following current
recommendations for SCP data analysis
[@vanderaa2023revisiting; @vanderaa2025scplainer], we will avoid
imputation whenever possible, using methods that handle missing values
directly.

Let's add gene symbols to the `rowData`, since proteins are identified by
UniProt accessions.

```{r}
# Add gene symbols to `rowData`
acc <- sub("-.*", "", rownames(prot)) # remove isoform suffixes
rowData(prot)$symbol <- AnnotationDbi::mapIds(
    org.Hs.eg.db::org.Hs.eg.db, keys = acc, keytype = "UNIPROT",
    column = "SYMBOL", multiVals = "first"
)
```

## Aggregating cells into metacells

To create metacells, we will first remove differences between TMT
sets with `limma::removeBatchEffect()` [@ritchie2015limma], while preserving
differences between time points. Since __limma__ fits linear models
to each protein using only observed values, missing values are kept as they
are. Then, we will identify groups of similar cells with a principal
component analysis (PCA) using the NIPALS algorithm (as implemented
in the __nipals__ package [@wright2026nipals]), which handles missing values
without imputation [@vanderaa2025scplainer]. To avoid restricting the
analysis to the most consistently detected (and, hence, highly abundant)
proteins, we will use all proteins detected in at least 30% of the cells.

```{r}
# Remove differences between TMT sets, preserving differences between days
mat <- limma::removeBatchEffect(
    assay(prot), batch = prot$Set, design = model.matrix(~ prot$SampleType)
)

# PCA with NIPALS using proteins detected in at least 30% of the cells
na_prop <- rowMeans(is.na(mat))
sum(na_prop <= 0.7)

pca <- nipals::nipals(t(mat[na_prop <= 0.7, ]), ncomp = 10, scale = FALSE)
pcs <- pca$scores

# Proportion of variance in the top 3 PCs explained by days and TMT sets
sapply(c(day = "SampleType", set = "Set"), function(covariate) {
    sapply(1:3, function(k) summary(lm(pcs[, k] ~ prot[[covariate]]))$r.squared)
})
```

The top principal components reflect differences between time points, not
between TMT sets. Now, we will cluster cells from each time point with
k-means, aiming at ~7 cells per metacell, and average the
abundances of cells in each metacell (ignoring missing values).

```{r}
# Cluster cells within each time point into metacells
cells_by_day <- split(colnames(prot), prot$SampleType)
metacell <- unlist(lapply(names(cells_by_day), function(day) {
    cells <- cells_by_day[[day]]
    km <- kmeans(pcs[cells, ], centers = round(length(cells) / 7), nstart = 10)
    setNames(paste0(day, "_mc", km$cluster), cells)
}))[colnames(prot)]

# Number of cells and TMT sets per metacell
summary(as.vector(table(metacell)))
summary(as.vector(tapply(prot$Set, metacell, function(s) length(unique(s)))))

# Average abundances in each metacell
mc_mat <- sapply(split(seq_along(metacell), metacell), function(i) {
    rowMeans(mat[, i, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
})
mc_mat[is.nan(mc_mat)] <- NA
dim(mc_mat)
mean(is.na(mc_mat))
```

Since metacells contain cells from different TMT sets, aggregation
substantially reduced the proportion of missing values. Let's
see how this affects correlations between proteins (using only proteins
with few missing values, so that correlations can be estimated
for cells).

```{r}
# Distribution of absolute correlations for proteins with few missing values
p <- na_prop <= 0.1
cor_cells <- cor(t(mat[p, ]), use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_mc <- cor(t(mc_mat[p, ]), use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

data.frame(
    level = rep(c("Cells", "Metacells"), each = sum(upper.tri(cor_cells))),
    abs_cor = abs(c(cor_cells[upper.tri(cor_cells)], cor_mc[upper.tri(cor_mc)]))
) |>
    group_by(level) |>
    summarise(mean = mean(abs_cor), median = median(abs_cor))
```

Absolute correlations increased substantially after aggregation, indicating that
sparsity was masking co-abundance signals. For network inference, we will
keep proteins detected in at least 80% of the metacells, as correlations
estimated from few observations are unreliable. Since correlations in
__BioNERO__ are calculated from complete data, we will replace the
remaining missing values (a small fraction) with protein means using
`BioNERO::replace_na()`. Unlike left-censored imputation, mean imputation does not
introduce artificial structure in the data, and it can only shrink
correlations toward zero (i.e., it is conservative). Then, we will create a
`GraphExperiment` object with metacells in columns, and store the
mapping between cells and metacells in the `metadata` slot.

```{r}
# Keep proteins detected in >=80% of the metacells and replace NAs
mc_mat <- mc_mat[rowMeans(is.na(mc_mat)) <= 0.2, ]
mean(is.na(mc_mat))
mc_mat <- BioNERO::replace_na(mc_mat, replaceby = "mean")

# Create metacell metadata
mc_md <- data.frame(
    row.names = colnames(mc_mat),
    day = sub("_mc.*", "", colnames(mc_mat)),
    n_cells = as.vector(table(metacell)[colnames(mc_mat)])
)

# Create `GraphExperiment` object
ge <- GraphExperiment(
    assays = list(abundance = mc_mat),
    rowData = rowData(prot)[rownames(mc_mat), ],
    colData = mc_md,
    metadata = list(metacells = data.frame(cell = colnames(prot), metacell))
)

ge
```

## Inferring a protein co-abundance network

Now, we will infer a signed hybrid co-abundance network with
__BioNERO__ [@almeida2022bionero]. As in use case 1, we will store the
full network (i.e., a complete weighted graph) in `rowGraphs`, with module
assignments and intramodular degrees as node attributes.

```{r}
# Get beta power
sft <- SFT_fit(ge, net_type = "signed hybrid", cor_method = "pearson")
sft$power

# Infer co-abundance network
net <- exp2gcn(
    ge, net_type = "signed hybrid", SFTpower = sft$power,
    cor_method = "pearson"
)
table(net$genes_and_modules$Modules)

# Create igraph object and add node attributes
g <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(
    net$adjacency_matrix, mode = "undirected", weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE
)
modules <- setNames(net$genes_and_modules$Modules, net$genes_and_modules$Genes)
V(g)$module <- modules[V(g)$name]
V(g)$kWithin <- net$kIN[V(g)$name, "kWithin"]

rowGraph(ge, "wgcna") <- g
```

We will also add a kNN graph of metacells to the `colGraphs` slot,
which can be used, for instance, to visualize or cluster metacells.

```{r}
# Build kNN graph of metacells from top PCs
mc_pcs <- prcomp(t(assay(ge, "abundance")), rank. = 10)$x
g_mc <- makeKNNGraph(mc_pcs, k = 5)
V(g_mc)$name <- colnames(ge)

colGraph(ge, "metacell_knn") <- g_mc

ge
```

## Exploring the co-abundance network

Module assignments are now available in `rowData`, and time points are
in `colData`. Thus, we can easily identify modules associated with EMT stages
by correlating module eigengenes with time points.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-dpi: 300

# Correlate module eigengenes with time points
me_trait <- module_trait_cor(ge, MEs = net$MEs, metadata_cols = "day")
plot_module_trait_cor(me_trait)
```

Let's look at the top hub proteins of the module most
negatively associated with day 0 (i.e., proteins with increased abundances
along EMT).

```{r}
# Get module most negatively correlated with day 0
emt_module <- me_trait |>
    filter(trait == "Day_0") |>
    slice_min(cor, n = 1) |>
    pull(ME) |>
    str_remove("^ME")
emt_module

# Top 20 proteins with the highest intramodular degree in this module
top_proteins <- rowData(ge) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    rownames_to_column("accession") |>
    filter(wgcna__module == emt_module) |>
    slice_max(wgcna__kWithin, n = 20)

top_proteins$symbol
```

Top hubs include several proteins involved in actomyosin contractility and
cytoskeletal remodeling (e.g., myosins, tropomyosins, filamins, and
transgelins), a hallmark of the transition to a mesenchymal phenotype.

Finally, let's visualize the top hubs of this module. Since `rowGraph()`
adds `rowData` variables as node attributes, gene symbols are readily
available for labeling.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-dpi: 300

# Subset object to keep top hubs and extract graph
g_hubs <- rowGraph(ge[top_proteins$accession, ], "wgcna")

# For visualization, keep only the strongest edges
g_hubs <- delete_edges(
    g_hubs, which(E(g_hubs)$weight < quantile(E(g_hubs)$weight, 0.5))
)

ggraph(g_hubs, layout = "fr") +
    geom_edge_link(aes(width = weight), alpha = 0.3, color = "grey50") +
    geom_node_point(aes(size = kWithin), color = emt_module) +
    geom_node_text(aes(label = symbol), repel = TRUE, size = 3.5) +
    scale_edge_width(range = c(0.2, 2)) +
    theme_graph(base_family = "sans") +
    labs(size = "Intramodular\ndegree", edge_width = "Adjacency")
```
